name: A Room of One's Own
author: Virginia Woolf
notes:
Sentences I liked

His expression suggested that he was labouring under some emotion that made him jab his pen on the paper as if he were killing some noxious insect as he wrote, but when he had killed it and that did not satisfy him, he must go on killing it, and even so some cause for anger and irritation remained.
They had been written in the red light of emotion and not in the white light of truth.

(“They” here refers to the books written by men on women.)

name: Geography of Bliss
author: Eric Weiner
notes:
Cafés are theaters where the customer is both audience and performer.

Netherlands

  • European cafés exist so you can linger without guilt — no wonder so many philosophers came out of them.
  • Dutch tolerance in everyday life: drugs, sex work and cycling are all legal.
  • Research by Ruut Veenhoven: tolerant people tend to be happy.

About happiness

  • Researchers call happiness “subjective well-being” (SWB) and measure it mostly through self-report surveys.
  • Happy feelings register in the parts of the brain that evolved most recently.
  • Noah Webster’s 1825 dictionary definition ties happiness to feeling good for the right reasons.
  • Many happiness findings run into reverse causality — do healthy people get happy, or happy people stay healthy?
  • Nozick’s Experience Machine: if you wouldn’t plug in for endless pleasure, there’s more to life than pleasure.
  • We have far more words for unhappiness than for happiness, in every language.
  • 🤣 The brooding café philosophers who decided the universe is an unhappy place.

Switzerland

  • Swiss reserve: they won’t point out what you don’t know, because that assumes ignorance.
  • The Swiss are happy because they work hard not to provoke envy — hence nobody talks about money.
  • Boredom, perfected and mass-produced; nothing is ever more than “pas mal”.
  • 🤯 Seventeenth-century Basel actually banned public laughter. Today the humourlessness is self-policing.
  • 😂 The Swiss love rules the way the Dutch love tolerance.
  • Where’s the bliss? Nature — biophilia, our innate bond with other living things.
  • Passports list your ancestral town; the Swiss gave us the word for homesickness, heimweh.
  • Honour-system huts in the Alps, direct democracy six or seven times a year — 😲 they once voted to raise their own taxes.
  • Weiner’s word for it: “conjoyment”.

Bhutan

  • The only country with a dress code for men.
  • Attention is an underrated word — life is empty without it.
  • Never colonised, so their hospitality comes without servility.
  • Gross National Happiness: measuring progress by people’s happiness, not the balance sheet.

name: The Myth of Sisyphus
author: Albert Camus
notes:
Chapter 1 — Absurdity and suicide

  • Camus opens with the one philosophical question he says comes before all others: whether life is worth living.
  • People end their lives both when life seems meaningless and when they’re defending a meaning — so it isn’t a simple equation.
  • The absurd isn’t just life lacking meaning; it’s the clash between our longing for meaning and a world that doesn’t answer.
  • That gap feels like exile, a divorce between a person and their life.
  • Camus rejects the either/or of “give up or carry on” and looks for a third way: living with the absurd, eyes open.

Chapter 2

Still reading.

name: Open
author: Andre Agassi
notes:
💡 The first chapter of this book is mind blowing.

Page 252

Agassi, sitting in Stuttgart with Brad, admits he hates tennis more than ever — and himself more. Then he reasons that millions of people do work they hate, and choose to respect it anyway.

Maybe doing what you hate, doing it well and cheerfully, is the point.

He tells Brad he’s all in.

name: Gut
author: Giulia Enders
notes:
How does pooping work?

  • There are two sphincters, each answering to a different nervous system.
  • The outer one obeys our conscious brain and stays shut when the moment is wrong.
  • The inner one belongs to the unconscious: “If it's gotta come out, it's gotta come out!”
  • When the two stop communicating, constipation can follow.
  • Childbirth can tear the delicate nerve fibres that let the two muscles talk to each other.

name: Freakonomics
author: Steven D. Levitt & Stephen J. Dubner
notes:
The three kinds of incentives

  1. Economic — money or property, like a fine for walking on the grass.
  2. Social — wanting to be liked; people cheat or shoplift more when no friends are watching.
  3. Moral — wanting to do the right thing, which economists see as getting the satisfaction of having done right.

The book’s claim: any measurable change in behaviour — a crime wave, a spike in ticket sales — traces back to a change in one of these three.

name: Buy Yourself the F*cking Lilies
author: Tara Schuster
notes:
• Faith is a practice, a habit you build — small loving rituals for your body and home teach you to feel the faith.
  • Build faith in yourself through physical activity, until taking on the next challenge feels like no big deal.
  • Pronoia — “the belief that people are secretly plotting for my well-being.” The opposite of paranoia: walk into a room assuming everyone already likes you.

Words I learnt

  1. Pirouette
  2. Shrouded with love
  3. Gunk under the nails
  4. Sommelier — a wine waiter

name: Invisible Women
author: Caroline Criado Perez
notes:
Worth is a matter of opinion, and opinion is informed by culture.
  • Who counts as “working class”? US coal mining — the 2016 election’s symbol — has about 53,000 jobs; the mostly female cleaning workforce is over 900,000 and paid far less.
  • Pg 189 — car design. A safety report counted only driver deaths. Since men usually drive when couples travel together, ignoring passengers largely means ignoring women.
  • Pg 198 — autoimmune diseases and vaccines. Women make up about 80% of autoimmune cases and react more strongly to vaccines; researchers have suggested sex-specific flu vaccines.
  • Pg 239 — GDP. GDP was shaped around the Second World War economy and deliberately left out unpaid household work. Much post-war “productivity growth” was really women’s work moving from the uncounted home into the counted market.

The failure to measure unpaid household work may be the biggest gender data gap of all. Counting it, the UK’s 2016 GDP would be around $3.9 trillion instead of $2.6 trillion, and India’s around $3.7 trillion instead of $2.3 trillion.

name: Traction
author: Gabriel Weinberg & Justin Mares
notes:
What is traction?

Quantitative evidence of customer demand — a couple of paying customers in enterprise software, maybe hundreds of thousands of users in consumer.

Traction is growth.

The ways a startup gets customers are called traction channels. There are 19 in total:

  1. Targeting blogs
  2. Publicity
  3. Unconventional PR
  4. Search engine marketing (SEM)
  5. Social and display ads
  6. Offline ads
  7. Search engine optimisation
  8. Content marketing
  9. Email marketing
  10. Engineering as marketing
  11. Viral marketing
  12. Business development
  13. Sales
  14. Affiliate programs
  15. Existing platforms
  16. Trade shows
  17. Offline events
  18. Speaking engagements
  19. Community building

The Bullseye Framework

Gabriel Weinberg’s write-up of the framework

name: The Lonely City
author: Olivia Laing
notes:
Fromm-Reichmann

The psychiatrist Frieda Fromm-Reichmann wrote that loneliness can’t be communicated, or even shared through empathy. One of her patients finally described it:

Hell is if you are frozen in isolation into a block of ice.

What I marked

  • Valerie Solanas and Andy Warhol: both drawn to the excessive and the rubbished, both upenders of what culture held dear.
  • Masks and loneliness — Maskenfreiheit, the freedom masks give: refusing to be seen dodges rejection, but also acceptance.
  • Changing something in the physical world can change the emotional landscape — maybe that’s what art is.
  • Laing on the gaze, appearance and gender, and finding herself somewhere between the binaries.
  • Being on the internet: wanting to be stimulated and private, engaged and numbed, to look and to be seen — easier through a screen.

Last lines

The cure for loneliness isn’t necessarily meeting someone. It’s learning to befriend yourself, seeing that much of what feels personal is really stigma and exclusion, and choosing kindness and solidarity.

name: Sempre Susan
author: Sigrid Nunez
notes:
You can tell how serious people are by looking at their books.
  • Sontag wore jeans and sneakers, refused to carry a purse and wondered why women burdened themselves with one.
  • She wouldn’t do anything to draw attention to her looks — yet she dyed her hair and wore Dior Homme.
  • Favourite words: boring, servile, exemplary, serious. Because of her, Nunez arranged her own books by subject and chronology.
  • It is harder for a woman to be taken seriously — Sontag’s rule number one was to stop being afraid of looking ambitious or “unladylike”.
  • An elitist, but not a snob: what mattered was how smart and curious you were, not your family.
  • A natural mentor — meet her once and you left with a reading list. She wanted her passions shared by everyone.
  • Besotted with moviegoing, always from a seat close to the screen.
  • Always a student, always young; friends compared her to a child, with an undiminished capacity for wonder.
  • She prized people who could make her laugh, but couldn’t tell a joke herself.
  • She hated being alone, even over morning coffee — and could be unkind when “correcting” friends, especially with an audience.

name: No Rules Rules
author: Reed Hastings & Erin Meyer
notes:
Favourite chapter — Bring it all to the world
Most questionable/radical chapter — The keeper test (7th)

Principle of infectious behaviour

Performance, good and bad, is contagious. A team of only high performers keeps pushing each other higher, so a leader’s first job is to build a team of stunning colleagues.

4A feedback guidelines

Giving feedback

  1. Aim to assist — give it with positive intent and explain how the change helps them or the company, not you.
  2. Actionable — focus on what the person can do differently.

Receiving feedback

  1. Appreciate — resist the urge to defend yourself; listen with an open mind.
  2. Accept or discard — you must consider all feedback, but acting on it is your call.

Belonging cues

When someone gives the boss candid feedback, respond with signals that they still belong — the more you do, the braver people get.

Freedom and responsibility

Freedom isn’t the opposite of accountability; it’s a path towards it.

On removing travel approvals

“Spend company money as if it were your own” backfired, so the whole expense policy became five words: Act in Netflix’s best interest. When a few people abuse freedom, deal with them — don’t add rules.

The pratfall effect

A mistake makes you more likeable only if people already think you’re highly competent; otherwise it costs you credibility.

name: The Socrates Express
author: Eric Weiner
notes:
1. How to get out of bed like Marcus Aurelius

  • What keeps us in bed isn’t the world, it’s our projections of it.
  • Staying under the covers is, in the end, a selfish act.
  • Duty comes from inside, obligation from outside. Marcus got up to work “as a human being”.

2. How to wonder like Socrates

Wonder is curiosity reclined, feet up, drink in hand.
  • “The unexamined life is not worth living.”
  • A good question reframes the problem — like the Indian brahmodya contests, which always ended in silence.

5. How to listen

Schopenhauer: good art quiets desire instead of stirring it.

6. How to see

Thoreau: hold off on naming what you see, and you’ll see more. Vision is our fastest sense, and the hardest to slow down.

name: Fahrenheit 451
author: Ray Bradbury
notes:
Stuff your eyes with wonder… live as if you’d drop dead in ten seconds.

The line I keep coming back to: see the world, ask for no guarantees and no security, and shake the great sloth out of its tree.

name: A Short History of Nearly Everything
author: Bill Bryson
notes:
• Penzias and Wilson were picking up the oldest light in the universe — photons from the big bang, stretched into microwaves, just as Gamow predicted.
  • They won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Physics, and only grasped what they’d found after reading about it in the New York Times.

Trivia — tune an old TV to a channel it doesn’t receive, and about 1% of the static is left over from the big bang.

name: The Consolations of Philosophy
author: Alain de Botton
notes:
My thoughts

I think it's a very cleverly structured book. Philosophy in it's core is to help people find answers to their questions, whether the theme of their questions be meta-physical or epistemological. The author uses insights from seven different philosophers to console the people on some life's basic problems and answers questions that stem out of just living a life.

1. Unpopularity — Socrates

What should matter isn’t how many people oppose us but how good their reasons are. An idea isn’t right because it’s unpopular, or wrong because it’s popular — only logic decides.

2. Not having enough money — Epicurus

We’re as bad at guessing what will make us happy as what will make us healthy. Money without friends, freedom and an examined life won’t make us happy; with those, the lack of a fortune won’t make us unhappy.

3. Frustration — Seneca

  • Anger comes from a correctable error of reasoning — we rage when we feel entitled to something we don’t get.
  • Shocks: life is both reliably continuous and capable of sudden catastrophe.
  • Anxiety: bad things will probably happen, but rarely as badly as we fear.
  • Wealth: neither fear nor despise poverty.

4. Inadequacy — Montaigne

  • Reading was the solace of his life.
  • Stop waging civil war on our bodies and accept them.
  • What counts as abnormal depends on time and place — we may cross borders in our minds.
  • Learning vs wisdom: only knowledge that helps us live well is worth much.
  • If a book bores you, put it down — and if it’s incomprehensible, blame the author.
  • Clever people should get their ideas from people even cleverer than they are. (In today's time what Tim Ferriss does is what Montaigne has asked us to do!)
  • Don’t let great books set the limits of your curiosity — they’re silent on too much.

5. A broken heart — Schopenhauer

  • The will-to-life drives us towards the ideal co-parent, which explains love’s blindness.
  • Rejection hurting so much is normal — it would be odd if it didn’t.
  • Art and philosophy turn our pain into knowledge.

6. Difficulties — Nietzsche

  • Fulfilment comes not from avoiding pain but from accepting it as a step towards anything good.
  • The glacier that carves a valley makes it fertile later.
  • Raphael was one of Nietzsche’s favourite painters.
  • He saw alcohol and Christianity as Europe’s two great narcotics — comfort chosen over growth.

name: Kitchen Confidential
author: Anthony Bourdain
notes:
My thoughts

It was an honest, raw and unapologetic account of his life, a life of a person in food in general, and inner secrets about the food business. His writing roars of his personality. You'll be a hater or an absolute fan of this man after reading it. Memoirs are my favourite genre and this is definitely one of the good ones!

Warnings from the book

  1. Never order fish on Mondays.
  2. Tuesday is the best night to eat out — the chef is rested and wants you happy.
  3. Avoid mussels in restaurants.
  4. Seafood on Sunday only if it isn’t an obvious way to offload ageing stock.
  5. Brunch!
  6. Don’t eat in a restaurant with filthy bathrooms. (This is obvious)
  7. Watch your waiter’s face — he knows.

What I marked

  • Line cooking is about consistency and repetition, not innovation.
  • A messy station means a messy mind — which is why dry side towels are hoarded like gold.
  • His famous disdain for vegetarians, and his warnings about chicken and shrimp.
  • Travel and eat without fear: try everything once.
An ounce of sauce covers a multitude of sins.

name: The Art of Loving
author: Erich Fromm
notes:
The prison of awareness

Anxiety of separateness

The experience of separateness arouses anxiety
  • Being separate means being cut off and helpless — it brings shame and guilt along with anxiety.
  • Fromm reads Adam and Eve’s shame not as prudishness but as the awareness of separateness without the reunion of love.
  • Our deepest need is to overcome separateness and leave the prison of our aloneness.

name: The Psychology of Money
author: Morgan Housel
notes:
🌟 Chapter 1

  • How much risk people take with money depends on when and where they grew up — personal history, not intelligence.
  • It’s hard for most of us to grasp why low-income households spend so much on lottery tickets — the reasoning isn’t ours.

🌟 Chapter 2

Luck: only about one in a million teenagers in 1968 went to a school with a computer. Bill Gates was one of them.

🌟 Chapter 5

Cash that keeps you from selling stocks in a crash earns far more than its interest rate. Compounding rewards good returns sustained without interruption.

🌟 Chapter 6

Disney story — TL;DR → The 83 minutes of Snow White movie saved the company.

Tail events drive most outcomes — staying calm through the recession months matters more than anything else.

🌟 Chapter 7 — Wealth vs rich

  • Spending money on things leaves you with the things, not the money.
  • Rich is current income; wealth is income not spent — options you haven’t taken yet.
  • Exercise is like being rich; turning down the treat meal is like being wealthy. Wealthy role models are hard to find because their wealth is hidden.

Chapter 10

Control over your time and options is one of the most valuable currencies there is.

Chapter 12

We underestimate how tail events compound — a chain from 9/11 to today’s student-loan burden.

🌟 Chapter 14

You don’t know today what you’ll want in the future, which makes long-term plans hard to keep.

Chapter 17

Pessimism is seductive.

Growth compounds slowly; destruction happens in an instant.

name: The Almanack of Naval Ravikant
author: Eric Jorgenson
notes:
On wealth

  • Getting rich is about knowing what to do, with whom and when — not hard work alone.
  • Seek wealth (assets that earn while you sleep), not money or status.
  • You won’t get rich renting out your time; own equity.
  • Play long-term games — all returns compound.
  • Escape competition through authenticity.
  • Leverage — code and media with no marginal cost — beats effort; judgment beats hours.
  • Set a high personal hourly rate and outsource anything below it.
  • Status games are zero-sum; wealth creation is positive-sum.
  • Build a unique character and luck finds you.

What is your definition of retirement?

Retirement is when you stop sacrificing today for an imaginary tomorrow.

On judgment

  • If you can’t decide, the answer is no.
  • Wisdom is knowing the long-term consequences of your actions.
  • “Clear thinker” is a better compliment than “smart”.
  • Load your head with mental models — evolution, game theory, Munger.

On happiness

  • Happiness is more about peace than joy.
  • About desire — every desire is a choice to be unhappy until you get it, so choose them carefully.
  • Life is a single-player game.
  • Being jealous only makes sense if you’d swap your whole life for theirs.
  • Get rid of the word “should”.
  • Self-discipline is a bridge to a new self-image.

name: Outline
author: Rachel Cusk
notes:
About breaking marriage

The narrator says she can’t give the reasons a marriage ended, because a marriage is “a system of belief, a story”. What was real was losing the house — leaving it meant they had stopped waiting.

She describes her son, who leaves the meeting place if you’re late and gets lost looking for you — when the only hope of being found is to stay where you agreed, and hold out.

name: How Proust Can Change Your Life
author: Alain de Botton
notes:
de Botton’s take on Proust.

  • Humans are remarkably dedicated to unhappiness — the frailty of our bodies, the fickleness of love, the deadening effects of habit.
  • Yet when death suddenly seems close, we fall back in love with life.
  • Which suggests it wasn’t life we’d lost the taste for, but our everyday way of living it — and that untried possibilities were there all along.

name: Cosmos
author: Carl Sagan
notes:
➡️ Erathosthenes was the first person accurately to measure the size of a planet. Earth. 2200 years ago.
  • Page 14 — the great minds of the Library of Alexandria: Hipparchus, Euclid, Herophilus, Heron, Apollonius and his conic sections — the curves planets and comets follow, Archimedes, Ptolemy, and Hypatia, the last light of the library.
  • Page 29 — plants filled the atmosphere with oxygen, a poison to early life. 99% of our atmosphere is biological: “The sky is made by life.”
  • Page 34 — evolution needs a balance between mutation and selection.
  • Page 105 — Venus and its runaway greenhouse effect: a warning for Earth.
  • Looking deep into space is looking back in time.
  • The library is our species’ communal memory, stored outside our genes and brains.
  • Page 351 — next to the real cosmos, superstition and pseudoscience look pale.

My insights

Gallelio and Kepler were born in the same generation.

The year Gallelio died, Newton was born.

name: One Hundred Years of Solitude
author: Gabriel García Márquez
notes:
She had that rare virtue of never existing completely except at the opportune moment.

This was my second attempt to read the book. This time around it gripped me with the words and proses. I finished about a forth of the book and thoroughly enjoyed. But I'm not going to continue reading it. This has nothing to do with the liking of the book but with the time it's taking me to hold to the story. This is one of those times when i don't want to invest into the story although i do want to know what happens to the family in the generations to come. It's a weird feeling. I like the book, but I don't like the time I'm spending to read and finish it. I want to find a better opportunity to get it done with. For now, 'Adios Amigo'.

name: Americanah
author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
notes:
Excerpts I marked

  • Ifemelu staring at a spilled Frappuccino stain on the train to avoid conversation.
  • Hamila’s knowing smile — welcome to a fellow African.
  • Obinze, who “wore their relationship so boldly, like a brightly colored shirt.”
  • Her joy becoming a restless thing, looking for a way to fly off.

My thoughts

Americanah got me hooked to it at page 3. Yes. I had never came across a book which could make this happen until i read Americanah. I had read 'We Should All be Feminists', although small, was a very powerful book. And so was Americanah. It told me a profound story, and a story which was essential to be told. It started with a high school love story which survived through the test of time and geographical distance. What i found really intriguing is how the theme of their love story lingers throughout the book even though how little was written in word about it. The book focused on immigration and it's challenges and on racism in America. I loved how bold and upfront Ifemelu was which translated into her successful blog. At the same time Obinze's demeanour and how boldly he wore his relationship with Ifemelu like a bright coloured shirt made me establish a strong belief in him.

name: The Intelligent Investor
author: Benjamin Graham
notes:
Are you an intelligent investor?

  • →The photograph talks about the insignificance of IQ/SAT scores.
  • →How a Hedge fund run my matheticians, novel prize winning economists lost 2billion dollars.
  • →How Sir Isaac Newton lost insane amount of money in South Sea Company.

Chapter 1 — Investment vs speculation

Not everyone in the stock market deserves to be called an investor.

➡️ From 1949 through 1958, the stock market earned one of it's highest 10-year returns in history.

name: Notes on a Nervous Planet
author: Matt Haig
notes:
• Late capitalism treats sleep as a rival — Netflix’s CEO said they’re competing with sleep.
  • Humans, like birds and sea turtles, have circadian rhythms.
  • Edison thought sleep made people lazy. He was wrong.

A note on wanting

Wanting something is fine, but “wanting is also lacking” — the more we want, the more happiness drips out of us.

Thich Nhat Hanh: excitement isn’t happiness; true happiness is based on peace.

The night sky

Why does the sky have such an effect? Looking up, we see stars as they were, sometimes since the Ice Age. Next to the sky, emails and deadlines shrink — and we’re looking at where we came from: we are made of starstuff.

name: Munnu: A Boy from Kashmir
author: Malik Sajad
notes: This book is a coming-of-age tale of Munnu who grew up in Indian administered part of Kashmir. The author has told daily life stories of his childhood which would have been normal had he not been in Kashmir. And because his home was in Kashmir every story(chapter) is tinged with conflicts and you are left with utter helplessness reading them. It becomes tough to go on reading the book.
